facts.title: Discovered in a London Museum
facts.text: Niobium was identified in 1801 by English chemist Charles Hatchett, who analyzed a black mineral sample stored in the British Museum. The rock had been sent from Connecticut decades earlier, so Hatchett named the new element 'columbium' (symbol Cb) in honor of Columbia, a poetic name for America. It remained one of the only elements first found in a museum collection rather than a mine or laboratory experiment.

facts.title: Named After a Mythical Princess
facts.text: For over a century chemists confused niobium with the very similar element tantalum. In 1844 the German chemist Heinrich Rose distinguished the two and renamed columbium 'niobium' after Niobe, the daughter of King Tantalus in Greek mythology. The pairing was a clever pun: since the new metal was tantalum's chemical twin, naming it for Tantalus's child captured their close family resemblance.

facts.title: One Element, Two Names
facts.text: The name battle lasted an astonishing 150 years, with American chemists and metallurgists insisting on 'columbium' while Europeans used 'niobium.' The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry finally settled the dispute in 1949, making 'niobium' the official name. Even today, some American metallurgical and steel industries still informally call it columbium.

facts.title: A Superconductor's Best Friend
facts.text: Niobium is the elemental metal with the highest superconducting critical temperature, becoming superconducting below about 9.3 kelvin (around minus 264 degrees Celsius). Its alloys niobium-titanium and niobium-tin are the workhorse superconductors of modern technology. They form the powerful electromagnets inside MRI machines and the magnets that steer particle beams in the Large Hadron Collider at CERN.

facts.title: Inside Your Smartphone's Atom Smasher
facts.text: Niobium-tin and niobium-titanium wires made it possible to build the colossal 8-tesla dipole magnets that bend protons around the 27-kilometer ring at CERN. Without superconducting niobium alloys cooled by liquid helium, modern particle physics on this scale would be impossible. The same family of magnets enables the high-field research tools that probe the structure of new materials and drugs.

facts.title: Rainbow Metal of Jewelry
facts.text: When niobium is anodized, a thin transparent oxide layer grows on its surface whose thickness controls which colors of light interfere and reflect back. By simply changing the voltage, jewelers produce vivid blues, purples, greens, and golds without any dyes or coatings. Because niobium is hypoallergenic and biocompatible, it is popular for body piercings, earrings, and even some surgical implants.

facts.title: The Tiny Ingredient in Strong Steel
facts.text: Adding just a few hundredths of a percent of niobium to steel dramatically increases its strength and toughness by refining the metal's grain structure. These 'high-strength low-alloy' steels make pipelines, car bodies, and skyscraper beams lighter yet stronger. Roughly 90 percent of all niobium mined ends up in steelmaking, often as the iron-rich alloy ferroniobium.

facts.title: Brazil Holds the Crown
facts.text: Brazil produces about 90 percent of the world's niobium, with a single enormous mine at Araxa in Minas Gerais supplying much of global demand. The element is concentrated in carbonatite rocks and extracted mainly from the mineral pyrochlore. This near-monopoly makes niobium a strategically important resource that many nations stockpile.

facts.title: Found in Moon Rocks
facts.text: Niobium is genuinely cosmic: traces of it have been measured in lunar samples brought back by the Apollo missions and in meteorites. On Earth it never occurs as a free metal because it bonds readily with oxygen, always appearing locked inside minerals like columbite and pyrochlore. Its abundance in the Earth's crust is modest, roughly 20 parts per million, similar to that of lithium.

facts.title: Resists Acid and Heat
facts.text: Niobium has an extremely high melting point of about 2,477 degrees Celsius and forms a tough, self-healing oxide film that makes it remarkably resistant to corrosion. This durability lets it survive inside chemical reactors and rocket-nozzle components exposed to punishing conditions. Its excellent biocompatibility, like its cousin tantalum, also makes it safe for pacemaker casings and orthopedic implants placed inside the human body.
